extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers researching the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of what a novel is: its defining features, historical development, major subgenres, narrative techniques, and production/media formats. Useful for readers or writers wanting canonical/descriptive criteria for identifying or producing novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictionality: a novel is an extended work of narrative fiction; 'Fictionality is most commonly cited as distinguishing novels from historiography.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary distinguishing feature from history, though the page notes this can be problematic (historical narratives have traditionally included inventions). Novels can nonetheless depict social, political, and personal realities with clarity not found in works of history (example: Ông cố vấn as a 'non-fiction' novel). Anti-pattern: treating 'novel' solely as factual history without recognition of invented fictionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary prose / prose style
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern novel usually makes use of a literary prose style; prose rather than verse became standard for the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While prose is standard, verse narratives can compete (examples: Byron's Don Juan, Pushkin's Yevgeniy Onegin) and there are verse novels (Vikram Seth's The Golden Gate). When judging/forming a novel, expect prose as normative but recognise legitimate verse exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience of intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels create an experience of intimacy for readers — a private, individualistic relationship between reader and text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intimate mode is cited as a characteristic distinguishing novels from more public or performative genres (example: The Tale of Genji). For writers, cultivating intimacy (interiority, private feelings, secret anxieties) is a common novelistic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length (long-form narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is today the longest genre of narrative prose fiction; length is a commonly cited attribute though precise boundaries are not fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes imprecision in defining length boundaries between short story, novella, and novel; E. M. Forster's guideline is at least fifty-thousand words. György Lukács links requirement of length to encompassing 'the totality of life.' Use word-count benchmarks (e.g., ~50,000+) as conventions rather than strict rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic depiction / social realism
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel often displays a realistic depiction of the state of a society (argument attributed to M. H. Abrams and Walter Scott).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism — believable social, political, and personal details — is a strong traditional criterion for novels (example: To Kill a Mockingbird). For forms that claim realism, judge fidelity to social detail, plausibility of social relations, and coherent depiction of a milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance versus novel distinction (marvellous/incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'romance' (as distinct from the novel) encompasses fictitious narratives that emphasize marvellous or uncommon incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating/producing a work, note emphasis: if the work foregrounds marvelous, extraordinary events and adventure, it may be operating in the romance tradition even if called a 'novel' (examples: Gothic novels, fantasy). The page cautions overlap: many works (Frankenstein, Lord of the Rings) are commonly called novels despite romance elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative experimentation and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels can employ experimental narrative techniques (e.g., rejection of continuous narration, metafictional address to the reader, stream-of-consciousness, unconventional visual elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy (addresses readers, visual experiments such as marbled or black pages), stream-of-consciousness techniques. Criterion for evaluation: coherence and purposefulness of experimentation, and whether technique serves thematic or psychological aims rather than mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific conventions (sentimental novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimental novels rely on emotional responses and feature scenes arranged to advance emotions rather than action; they valorize 'fine feeling'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a sentimental novel, emphasise the ability to evoke and manage readers' emotional responses; assess arrangement of scenes to heighten tenderness/distress. Anti-pattern: confusing sentimentality with mere melodrama or manipulative pathos without moral/character function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical and didactic novel criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophical novel uses fiction to explore philosophical ideas; novels have a tradition of embedding didactic or utopian argument (examples: More's Utopia, Voltaire's Candide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively narrative and character embody or interrogate philosophical positions; judge balance between argument and narrative vitality (didacticism becomes liability if it overwhelms story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical novel: research and use of documentary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical novels may combine historical research and imaginative reconstruction; Walter Scott used documentary sources alongside marvelous incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for historical fiction include plausibility of historical setting, fidelity to important facts where relevant, and transparent use of research to enrich rather than distort narrative. Scott's method: research + imaginative re-evaluation of history — effectiveness judged by how research informs character and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/structure subtypes (epistolary, serial, novella relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels include various structural subforms — epistolary (collections of letters), serialized publication, multi-volume novels, and relations to novella/short forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should consider how chosen form affects pacing, viewpoint reliability, and reader engagement; e.g., epistolary form foregrounds subjective perspective and document framings, serialization affects cliffhangers and episodic plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/production context and medium influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of printing, cheap paper, and publishing institutions shaped the novel's development; modern developments include audiobooks, web novels, ebooks, and graphic novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating novels, account for medium constraints/opportunities (length expectations, serializability, visual integration in graphic novels, listening experience for audiobooks). The page emphasises that technological and market contexts materially shape form and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic, sensation, and romance subgenre conventions (grotesque, thrill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic and sensation romances exploit the grotesque, thrills, horror, or scandal; they prioritize emotional and sensational effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate use of setting, atmosphere, and plot devices to generate suspense and horror; beware of hollow shock devices that lack psychological or thematic depth. The tradition includes authors like Walpole, Radcliffe, and early Gothic exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and parody in novelistic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical romances and novels use parody, burlesque, or satirical inversion of genres (e.g., Don Quixote's burlesque of chivalric romance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the target and subtlety of satire, the novel's comic mechanics, and whether parody clarifies or obscures thematic intent. Successful satire integrates critical perspective with narrative interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on interiority and modern subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern novels often foreground interiority: personal views, intimate feelings, secret anxieties and conduct, reflecting an individualistic consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging modernist or realist novels, focus on depth and fidelity of psychological portrayal, use of free indirect discourse or interior monologue, and whether interiority contributes to thematic complexity rather than mere self-indulgence.
